digest.top_line: RAVES QOL: post-RP adjuvant RT put severe urinary leakage at 16% vs 2% in men who never needed RT (5 yr, p=0.01).
digest.tldr: Prostate carried the day, and it is a fossa-RT toxicity read, not an efficacy one: RAVES' protocol-planned QOL secondary quantifies what adjuvant RT costs men who would never have needed it, while timing from RP to sRT showed no QOL association at 3-5 yr. Caveats matter: 3D-CRT era, exploratory, 64% completion.

verdict.rationale: Protocol-planned secondary QOL analysis of a randomised trial; exploratory, unadjusted for multiplicity. Supports the early-salvage strategy the RAVES/GETUG-17/RADICALS primary results already established.
verdict.audience: Post-RP prostate ca with adverse pathology or rising PSA, Gleason 7 dominant

studies.significance: The QOL penalty tracks receiving RT, not when you give it: severe leakage was 16% aRT vs 13% in salvage men who were irradiated (p=0.7), and time from RP to RT was flat across every domain at 3-5 yr. So delaying salvage buys nothing functionally; the benefit is the 52% of sRT men never irradiated at all.
studies.monday_clinic: In a man with adverse pathology after RP and an undetectable PSA, this supports surveillance with early salvage on PSA rise rather than adjuvant fossa RT; it does not address men needing ADT or pelvic nodal coverage, who were excluded.

primary_endpoint.name: Minimal clinically important change in EORTC QLQ-PR25 domains
primary_endpoint.stat_detail: severe urinary leakage at 5 yr, aRT vs no RT, p=0.01

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Protocol-planned secondary analysis of the TROG 08.03 phase 3 noninferiority RCT. **166 randomised to aRT, 167 to sRT**; median follow-up 6 yr in both arms (IQR 4-7.1). Complete-case, no imputation.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Adverse pathology after radical prostatectomy (positive margins, extraprostatic extension, or seminal vesicle invasion). **82% Gleason 7**, 3% Gleason 8, 12% Gleason 9. Median age 63.8 vs 63.9 yr (p = 0.9).

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **64 Gy in 32 fractions to the prostate fossa** in both arms, aRT within 6 mo of surgery, sRT triggered at PSA ≥0.2 ng/ml and delivered within 4 mo. **Concurrent ADT and pelvic nodal RT were not permitted**, and most men were treated with 3D-CRT rather than IMRT.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Primary:** proportion reaching an MCIC, defined as a **>0.5 SD decline from baseline** on each QLQ-PR25 domain (urinary, bowel, sexual activity, sexual functioning). Secondary: severe individual symptoms ("quite a bit"/"very much"), QLQ-C30 global health, and regression of QOL on time from RP to RT.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Only **48% of the sRT arm (80/167) ever received RT**, which is what drives the arm-level difference. Against salvage men who were irradiated, aRT showed **no consistent difference** in any domain, and the sRT group actually reported more sexual-activity MCIC at 3 yr (58% vs 32%, p = 0.004) and 4 yr (65% vs 43%, p = 0.038), with older median age at RT (66.8 vs 63.9, p = 0.01) and more likely ADT exposure confounding that read.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: GETUG-AFU 17 and RADICALS reported clinician-graded late GU toxicity favouring salvage, but neither used a validated patient-reported instrument out to 5 yr, so cross-trial comparison of continence is unreliable. The 16% severe leakage here sits inside the **10-20% CTCAE grade 2 incontinence** range from earlier clinician-rated series.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents post-RP men with adverse pathology treated to 64 Gy/32 fx fossa-only RT without ADT. Does not represent men receiving pelvic nodal RT, concurrent ADT, hypofractionation, or PSMA PET-directed salvage.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Exploratory with **no multiplicity correction**, so the authors read sustained trends rather than single comparisons. The aRT-versus-no-RT contrast is **not a randomised comparison** (it conditions on not recurring), 5 yr QOL completion was **64% (214/333)**, and comorbidities and medications were not modelled.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The bowel finding is the softest number on the card: the MCIC threshold worked out to **2.2 points on a 100-point scale** against an instrument whose minimum possible change is 8.3 points, so a single one-point shift on one of four questions crosses it. The urinary leakage signal is more durable, consistent across 4 and 5 yr, and it is the one that should enter a consent discussion.

studies.interpretation:
The RAVES primary result already settled the oncological question: adjuvant fossa RT did not beat early salvage on freedom from biochemical progression, and GETUG-AFU 17, RADICALS and the pooled meta-analysis pointed the same way. What remained genuinely open was the mechanism of the QOL advantage that guidelines assume when they recommend salvage. Two explanations were live. Either delay itself is protective, letting continence recover before the fossa is irradiated, or the benefit is entirely a numerator effect: salvage spares a subset of men from ever being treated, and the men who do get treated fare the same whenever they get it. This analysis is the cleanest attempt to separate those, and it lands firmly on the second.

The evidence for that is the contrast that gets least attention on the card. Among men who actually received RT, adjuvant versus salvage produced no consistent difference in urinary, bowel or sexual domains from 1 to 5 yr after treatment, and severe urinary leakage at 5 yr was 16% versus 13% (p = 0.7). Univariable regression of each domain on time from surgery to RT returned coefficients that were not significant at 3, 4 or 5 yr, with intervals spanning zero in every domain. Only 48% of the salvage arm ever needed RT. That is the whole effect. A reader who has been telling men that waiting protects their continence has been offering the right recommendation for the wrong reason, and the framing matters when a man with a positive margin asks why he is not being treated now.

Two findings deserve unequal confidence. The urinary leakage signal is the one to carry into clinic: it is present at both 4 yr (12% vs 2%) and 5 yr (16% vs 2%) against men who never received RT, it is directionally concordant with the clinician-graded late GU toxicity RAVES reported originally, and its magnitude sits inside the 10-20% grade 2 incontinence range from prior series. Consistency across timepoints and across two independent measurement modes is what makes an exploratory finding believable. The bowel finding is far weaker than its p value suggests. The MCIC threshold computed out to 2.2 points on a 100-point scale for a four-question, four-point Likert composite whose smallest possible move is 8.3 points, so a single one-step change on one question counts as clinically important. The authors are candid that a doubled threshold would not change the proportions, which is a defence of stability rather than of clinical meaning.

The result should also travel poorly forward in one specific way. Most of this cohort was treated with 3D-CRT, and IMRT is now standard for the fossa with lower rectal dose, so the bowel detriment is an upper bound on what a contemporary patient faces. The urinary finding transfers more directly, since continence after fossa RT is not obviously a conformality problem. Neither finding speaks to the treatment most post-RP men now receive: ADT and pelvic nodal coverage were both prohibited in RAVES, and SPPORT established that intensification improves freedom from progression, so a man treated to the modern standard is being offered a toxicity profile this trial never measured. Hypofractionation, tested in NRG-GU003, is the same gap. The honest summary is that this confirms the strategy while measuring a regimen that is drifting out of use.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The QOL penalty tracks receiving RT, not when: severe leakage was 16% aRT vs 13% in irradiated salvage men (p=0.7), and time from RP to RT was flat in every domain at 3-5 yr. Delay buys nothing functionally. Dose was 64 Gy/32 fx fossa-only, 3D-CRT era, so the bowel signal overstates IMRT-era risk.
significance_by_specialty.surgonc: For consent after RP with adverse pathology, the number to quote is 16% severe urinary leakage at 5 yr in irradiated men versus 2% in those never irradiated. Deferring RT until PSA rise does not soften that penalty for the man who ultimately needs it; it spares the 52% who never do.
